The median here is $1,106 a year (single-family primary home, premium plus fees, in force August 31, 2026). That is 12% below the New York median of $1,261 and 4% above the U.S. median of $1,066. It is 15th lowest of 48 New York counties with 100+ priced policies.

By ZIP (the 18 with 25+ priced policies), the median ranges from $447 (11218 New York) to $1,305 (11229 New York).

Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside those zones, a lender may still require it.

45.8% of Kings County's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones. That is a share of insured policy units, not of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home.

Of the NFIP claim dollars paid here (1978–2026), 27.4% went to claims rated outside high-risk zones A and V. That uses the zone on each claim, not today's map, and leaves out claims with no zone.

Zone AE (high-risk)8,53845.8%
Zone C2601.4%
Other high-risk zones (A05, VE, A08)100.1%
Other low-risk or unclassified zones40.0%

Policy records keep the code they were rated with, so older labels such as A1 to A30 are counted on their own. Every zone starting with A or V is high-risk; A1 to A30 and AE are the same kind of area (44 CFR §64.3).

Insured units by the zone each policy is rated in. How this is counted What each means: zone AE, zone X, zone VE.

Flood insurance cost in Kings County, New York

In Kings County, single-family primary-home NFIP policies typically cost about $1,106 a year ($92 a month), fees included. Half pay between $722 and $1,380. To check a quote, use the checker at the top.

A quarter pay under $722 · Typical $1,106 · A quarter pay over $1,380 · A tenth pay $1,934 or more

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus the federal policy fee, reserve fund assessment and HFIAA surcharge), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half of policies, from 3,719 single-family primary-home policies. These are existing policies, many still below FEMA's full-risk price.

The NFIP also offers policies for renters and businesses. The median here is for single-family primary-home policies, not businesses or second homes. Renting? See what renters pay.

Source: floodsmart.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy. Bought while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, it can start at closing if the insurer is paid within 10 days (30 if the lender, title company or settlement attorney pays).

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageCan start at closing, if paid in time
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage. Does homeowners insurance cover flooding? To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim), and send a proof of loss (your signed, sworn statement of the amount you are claiming) within 60 days of the flood (44 CFR 61, App. A(1), Art. VII). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster.

Wait exceptions, exclusions, premium increases and surcharges, aid, appeals, rebuilding and closing rules: the NFIP rules in full.

Your state's insurance regulator: New York Department of Financial Services.

Source: floodsmart.gov, agents.floodsmart.gov, fema.gov, ecfr.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Flood insurance claims in Kings County, New York: what floods pay out

Floods in Kings County have led to 6,152 NFIP flood claims and $327.6 million in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2012, 2021 and 2023.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2012 ($304,684,259), 2021 ($6,527,978), 2023 ($3,849,332). Total paid $327,630,683. Totals for 2025 and 2026 are not final while their claims stay open. How this is counted

Outside the high-risk zones: 643 claims here from losses 2016–2025 have a flood zone on the claim. Of these, 67.0% were rated outside zones A and V (zones X, B, C and D). They got 47.8% of the dollars paid on these claims. The zone is the one on each claim, not today's map; claims with no zone on them are left out.

Do flood claims here actually pay out?

Most do: 84.8% of claims in Kings County paid something. The average paid claim was $63,139 (all years, in dollars of the day, not adjusted for inflation).

Typical claim: the median paid building claim was $32,599; Hurricane Sandy alone paid $306.1 million including code-upgrade (ICC) pay, which pulls the average up.

  • Average paid claim, incl. code-upgrade (ICC) pay$63,139New York: $39,732

FEMA's claim records give a reason when a building claim has no recorded payment, such as damage less than the deductible, not an actual flood, seepage or backed-up drains. The average is over claims that paid something and includes Increased Cost of Compliance payments (help to elevate or rebuild to code), which the yearly totals above leave out. Dollars are as paid at the time, not adjusted for inflation; a single home can file across several floods over the years. All years, records FEMA coded as entered in error left out (the claims page uses losses from 2020 on, so its shares differ). FEMA's data has no open or closed field, so a recent claim with no payment may still be paid.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for at least 63.8% of the 2,444 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 2,444 policies reporting one)63.8%New York: 53.6%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)88.6%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 4,945 claims paid with a damage figure)5.3%

The two shares have different bases: insured-to-the-maximum counts every single-family policy with the full building limit; the rebuilding-cost share counts only the policies that report a rebuilding cost. Homes insured for less than their own rebuilding cost can also fall short. How this is counted

The NFIP pays the cost to rebuild (not a depreciated value) only for a single-family home that is your principal residence and is insured for at least 80% of its full rebuilding cost, or for the $250,000 maximum.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies; FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective August 31, 2026; retrieved November 14, 2026.

What does it cost in my flood zone?

From about $934 a year (Zone X) to $1,320 (Zone AE) here. Your zone is on your lender's flood determination or FEMA's map; find its row below.

Flood zoneMedian / yrPriced policies
Zone X$9342,320
Zone AE$1,3201,385

What the zone codes mean (44 CFR §64.3): A, AE and A1–A30 are high-risk; AO and AH are high-risk with shallow flooding; A99 is high-risk behind a flood barrier FEMA treats as complete; V, VE and V1–V30 are coastal high-risk, flooded by tides with fast-moving water (velocity); B and X are areas of moderate flood hazard, C and X areas of minimal hazard; D has possible but undetermined flood hazards. A 1 percent or greater chance a year works out to a 26% or greater chance of at least one such flood over 30 years.

Zones with fewer than 50 priced single-family policies are omitted. Your own premium still depends on elevation and coverage.

Source: ecfr.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

How Kings County appears in the national research papers

Each paper sorts the U.S. counties with enough records by one measure into five groups of about equal size, from highest fifth to lowest fifth. A group is a position in a list, not a grade or a prediction.

  • Flood damage over building coverage: NFIP claims by county: Of 155 paid single-family primary-home claims with recorded damage and coverage here (losses 2016–2025), 0.0% (90% range 0.0–1.7%) had recorded building damage over the building coverage. That ranks in the lowest fifth of 268 U.S. counties listed.
  • Outside the zone: paid flood claims rated outside high-risk zones: Of 447 claims with a payment and a rated zone here (losses 2016–2025), 73.2% (90% range 69.6–76.5%) were rated outside zones A and V. That ranks in the highest fifth of 364 U.S. counties listed.
  • Building deductibles on record: NFIP single-family homes by county: Of 3,701 single-family primary-home policy units with a known building deductible here, 13.1% (90% range 12.2–14.0%) had a building deductible of $5,000 or more on record. That ranks in the second-lowest fifth of 1,793 U.S. counties listed.
  • Peak month of NFIP claims by county: Of 643 NFIP claims with a month of loss here (losses 2016–2025), 65.5% (90% range 62.3–68.5%) were in their county's peak month. That ranks in the second-highest fifth of 416 U.S. counties listed. Peak month: September, over half of it from September 2021 alone. At random, 10.2% of claims would land in one month at this size, so the ranking uses the share above that.
  • The gap to FEMA's full-risk premium: NFIP single-family homes by county: Of 3,719 single-family primary-home policies priced both ways here, 25.2% (90% range 24.0–26.4%) had a premium at least $100 a year below FEMA's full-risk premium. That ranks in the middle fifth of 1,793 U.S. counties listed.

How much flood risk is here?

Relatively High for coastal flooding and Very High for inland (river) flooding, by FEMA's county rating. That compares this county with others; it is not a forecast for your address.

  • Coastal flood risk rating (FEMA)Relatively High
  • Inland flood risk rating (FEMA)Very High

FEMA's rating weighs modeled loss with social vulnerability and community resilience. It is not a prediction for your home, and it can differ from the loss percentile below. FEMA's model puts yearly flood loss here at roughly $2.7 million for coastal flooding and $181.2 million for inland flooding. It counts buildings, people and farmland valued in dollars, insured or not, so it runs far above insurance payouts. A separate FEMA measure, loss per dollar of building value, is higher here than in about 53% of U.S. counties for coastal flooding and about 9% for inland flooding. How this is counted

Source: FEMA — National Risk Index (flood). Data: NRI December 2025 release; retrieved November 14, 2026.

Do the same homes flood again here?

Yes: FEMA's disaster-aid records hold 2,173 records from homes here that FEMA lists as flood-damaged in more than one declared disaster; 12 records are from homes FEMA's disaster-aid data flags as severe repeat-loss (SRL).

  • Disaster-aid records on repeat-flood homes2,173
  • Records from homes flagged severe repeat-loss (SRL)12

These count records, one per home per declared disaster, not distinct homes, and FEMA does not mark flood damage on every record. How this is counted

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Individual Assistance Multiple-Loss Flood Properties. Data: FEMA's current multiple-loss list; retrieved November 14, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $191.4 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $5,596 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Only disasters counted in the flood-disaster card are included; their aid can still cover wind or tornado damage from the same storm. Disasters for COVID, fire, winter storms or tornadoes alone are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved November 14, 2026.
